speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first is to protect the public from the growing threat of terrorist actions to events that take place in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members will be aware of the threat of terrorism around the world and in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We increasingly see a modus operandi where terrorists target soft targets as one of the main modes of attack.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are large events with large crowds with limited protection, or public buildings which are less secure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You have seen that over the past two years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You had in November 2015 the attack in Paris where they attacked a cafe, football match and concert.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In June of last year, you had the attack in Nice.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In December of last year, you have the Christmas Market attack in Germany.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of course, you have the New Year's Eve shooting at an Istanbul nightclub, with 39 persons dead.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nightclubs, public events, cafes, football events and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In terms of how the Government has responded, we have taken significant steps.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have put in more cameras, increased vigilance with technology.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have new capabilities with the Emergency Response Teams.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have indicated that they are trained to be at any place in Singapore within a certain number of minutes and they understand the local terrain very well, including the buildings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have also conducted major exercises to see what the gaps are and continuously upgrade and sharpen our skills.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In addition, we have also launched the SGSecure movement to bring in the population, and our intention is the entire population has got to come into this and work with the Government in a partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fact is that terrorists have imposed a cost on society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the Government and the taxpayers are paying the cost.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, business owners, event organisers will have to bear a part of this cost.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is what the first part is about.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Not all of it, but a part of it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, why do we have to regulate security for events?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When there is a risk of a potential terrorist attack at an event, and the risk is assessable as potentially dangerous, then it is really in the public interest that the Government does something about it, that the necessary security measures are taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The practical issue then becomes one of balancing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What measures do we put in, where do we draw the line, and how do we calibrate so that the measures are reasonable and practicable?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are usually events of major and national significance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To give some examples, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) 2009 meetings in Singapore, Southeast Asian Games Opening and Closing Ceremonies, National Day Parade, events like that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police require a wide range of powers to ensure event security to protect the public, in events of such significance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those powers include the power to inspect personal property, search people, prohibit certain items from being taken into the event area, security screening, refusing entry into special events and also issuing directions to event organisers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we know, today's threats are not limited to these sorts of events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: From my earlier illustrations, you have seen they attack concerts, they attack festivals, any kind of gathering.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, we cannot subject all these events to the kind of security or rules that we require, say, for the National Day Parade.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You cannot let it go completely unprotected nor can you impose the kind of security that you do for the kind of events I have talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When we strike a balance, we must remember and accept that when you put in security measures, they do deter attackers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, in November 2015, the terrorists wanted to go into the stadium.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But they were deterred because there were security checks, so they detonated outside and that caused much less loss of lives.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After the attacks in Berlin and Nice, questions were raised as to why there were no higher security measures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Singapore, in February this year, we had the Guns N' Roses concert at the Changi Exhibition Centre reputed to have 50,000 people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Concerns have been raised as to why there were no added security measures as this is the kind of events that can be targeted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, what are the gaps today and how do we deal with them?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you have events with large crowds, higher risk, there has got to be adequate security, and there has got to be legal powers for the Police to direct that some security measures be put in that are considered adequate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is the approach we are going to take?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the Police can then direct that the event organisers take special steps, security measures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of course, if the event organiser refuses to comply with the directions of the Police, then it has to be a non-compliance with the law.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The intent of this framework which I have just explained − notifying the Police, allowing the Police to give directions, and making non-compliance an offence − is to make sure that the basic security measures are in place, and also allow the Police to direct further security measures, for example, if there is credible or a reasonable basis to believe that there are specific or generalised threats.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are assessments that the Police have to make.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, let me deal with the main provisions of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members will note from clause 3 of the Bill, it requires organisers to give the Police notice of intention if they expect the crowd size to be above a prescribed size.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will a period prescribed and a notification has got to take place in the context of the prescribed period.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Events that meet the crowd size thresholds will then be declared as special events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In making the declaration, the Police will assess if the event is at potential risk of a terrorist attack or a public order incident.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What types of events do we intend to prescribe once the Bill comes into force?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason for making a distinction between public and private events is that one assumes that, for a private event, the organisers know who they are inviting.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And because it is by invitation only, then there is no wide public invitation and, therefore, potentially lesser profile.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, of course, I am just setting the general principles.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The specific cases will vary and the Commissioner will have to make that assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the event organisers would try to make an estimate based on the facts available to them, such as the size of the venue, past events of a similar nature, ticket sales and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The organiser makes the best estimate he or she can.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if the crowd size exceeds what they estimated, then, of course, that is not an offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have got to draw a line somewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Take into consideration, first, the seating capacity of major event venues in Singapore and also looking at the scheduled landscape of events that we have in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at the Singapore Indoor Stadium, it can hold 7,000 to 8,000 people when used for concerts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Star Performing Arts Centre can accommodate up to 5,000 people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How many events would this apply to, based on past precedents?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And remember these 200 public events today have already put in place many of these security measures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is being done is to give the Police the directive power.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What we have today is a system where the Police work with the organisers and the organisers voluntarily do this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill will effectively give the Police the power to direct.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we want to encourage people to organise events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not want to stifle the vibrancy of events being held in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, we have to recognise that the worldwide impact of terrorism is imposing costs on everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That gives enough time for the Police to make an assessment, engage with the organisers on the security requirements and for the organisers to put in place the security requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because the Police have to make an assessment, then they have got to go back to the organisers and say "we need you to do these things", and the organisers need time to go and put in place those requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, sometimes, it is not possible to give such notice.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, clause 3 will actually require the Commissioner to accept shorter notice, if he is reasonably satisfied that an earlier notice could not have been given.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is also the power to declare an event as a special event by the Commissioner of Police.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 8 of the Bill will repeal and re-enact section 21.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When it is necessary to preserve the public order and the safety of individuals involved in the event, as well as other persons, and also where it is necessary to avoid disruptions to the event.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What would the Commissioner have to consider in declaring events as a special event?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has got to look at the size of the event.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has got to look at the experience and expertise of the organisers and he has got to look at the other factors, including threat assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In practice, how is the Commissioner likely to exercise this power?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think he will exercise this power when an event is likely to attract a very large crowd and he assesses it to be at a higher risk of a terror attack or a public order incident.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are iconic events that can be targets.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Once the Commissioner declares an event to be a special event, he will issue directions to the event organisers to put in place the security measures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He will use section 30, which is an existing provision that applies to special events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Currently, the Minister declares them to be special events under section 30, but he will use the powers under section 30.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 9 of the Bill will amend section 30 to clarify examples of written directions that the Commissioner can give.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us say an event has been declared a special event or enhanced security special event.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police will then discuss the security plan with the organisers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police will then issue directions to the event organisers to put in place the agreed or hopefully agreed security measures, which could include setting up of barricades, engaging security officers by having clear signage.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that is likely to apply to the majority of special events which are events which attract large crowds.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And you have seen how vehicle-borne threats can cause chaos.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If for some reason that event venue cannot be secured against security risks, the Police may require the venue to be changed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The event may be cancelled or postponed if it is unsafe for it to continue.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That could be due to an imminent threat or severely inadequate security and also inadequate crowd management arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police may also require the organisers to inform the participants, the public at large, regarding some aspects of how the event is going to be conducted, for example, to come earlier because of security screening.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that could include, if the event organisers are not putting in the security, the Police can put in the security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can also recover the costs and expenses incurred in doing so, as a civil debt owed to the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But stepping in to implement the security requirements is really an option of last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it is important to have this option in case you have organisers who just go ahead, ignore everything and have a large-scale event without adequate security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 10 will make it an offence for anyone to willfully obstruct any Police Officer or the Commissioner in the exercise of his powers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Supposing a Commissioner declares an event be a special event, then the powers that are exercisable in relation to the participants and members of the public under sections 24 to 29 and section 32A will not apply.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As the participants and members of the public at a special event will not be subject to these powers, the declaration of the special event by the Commissioner does not have to be gazetted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Generally, these are events of major national or international significance which have previously been declared as special events under this Act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The powers that are exercisable in relation to these events remain largely unchanged.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we have to demarcate the events which the Minister will declare as special events from those declared by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Minister will give directions to the Commissioner to refer certain events or a class of similar events to the Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And then the Minister will decide whether or not to declare these events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Any declaration made by the Minister must be published in the Gazette because the powers do affect members of the public in and around the vicinity of the special event.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have consulted the People's Association, Football Association of Singapore and event companies providing entertainment, as well as sporting events, and event security and logistics providers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Based on the feedback we have received, we will develop guidelines for event organisers on what procedures they need to adopt to notify the Police, and also what security measures are required for a typical event, and what sort of additional security measures that might be imposed, depending on the threat assessment and the nature of the event.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In doing this, obviously, the private security industry is an important partner to help us implement this framework.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are working with the tripartite partners to develop what is being called the Industry Transformation Map (ITM) for the Private Security Industry.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we will focus on innovation, technology and upgrading the jobs and skills of the officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hopefully, that will help the private security industry meet the demands in the years ahead because you are going to have security officers who need to be professional in handling this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second part of this Bill relates to the amendment to section 7(2), to prevent foreigners from using Singapore to promote political causes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Police have previously rejected permit applications by non-Singaporeans to organise events, for example, the Bersih-related events at the Speakers' Corner.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those events, where a permit is applied for, will be assessed carefully, case-by-case, by the Police.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill also seeks to ensure that Singapore will not be used as a platform by foreigners to further political causes, especially those that are controversial or divisive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given the current regional and global security environment, the proposed changes are timely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The recent attack along Westminster Bridge in London has once again emphasised the need for us to always remain vigilant and alert for any form of attacks on our citizens, including our security forces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am glad that the Bill aims to further strengthen our security measures to better protect our people, particularly at large-scale events where many will gather.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I have some areas of concern for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would issues related to race and religion fall under this term?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Ministry share where the boundaries or the out-of-bounds markers are?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps some examples would be useful to provide a better understanding of what constitutes "public controversy" under section 7.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, the new security measures will inevitably mean that we will need more security officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This security workforce is supplemented by a significant number of Malaysians.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Recently, we heard that concession has been given to some security companies to hire Auxiliary Police Officers from new sources, such as Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must build up our pool of local security professionals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to establish pipelines of suitable locals into our security industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, we must work on improving standards and enhancing training of our security workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, we have seen a steady increase in the number of large-scale special events.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important for our security officers to be well-trained, well-equipped and well-informed to handle the ever-changing security threats at such events.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They must be properly trained and be kept up to date on the latest security threats and tactics used by those who intend to cause us harm.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These modules are delivered by different training providers and some security companies have even set up their own training centres.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider consolidating the various training resources and establish a centralised training institute for all security officers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would allow basic training to be structured and ensure a level of consistency in delivery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would also allow for regular review of the training curriculum and provide a platform for continuous training for our security workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To attract more Singaporeans to join the security profession, the job scope of security officers should progress beyond basic guarding and move towards more skills-based and knowledge-based security operations, so that the value of the job and the image of our security officers can improve over time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to expand on this and create multiple career tracks for our security officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We know, for example, that the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) West trains students who can set up and monitor remote command centres.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But today, this task requires a security supervisor under the single-track PWM and he needs to have four years of experience, that is, two years as a security officer and another two years as a senior security officer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this is on top of the WSQ prerequisites at each rung and each level.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although exceptions can be given, and are given on appeal, most ITE graduates from this course will find it hard to join the industry and practise what they had been trained for as they do not qualify.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could we explore a parallel career track for security technologists?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For many security companies, the need for more security officers will add to the business costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But this is also an opportunity for the industry to work together to optimise our limited manpower resources.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Security companies need to invest more in risk assessment and smarter use of technologies to augment physical bodies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we use sensors and surveillance cameras in place of human beings to guard a locked door?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we leverage technology to secure our perimeters instead of a patrol team?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Do we need to patrol both sides of the same perimeter fence because they belong to two different owners?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is preventing us from optimising the use of our security manpower?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, there is a lack of common standards for security technology.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has resulted in buyers installing excessive, and sometimes over-priced, systems that they do not need.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Police consider working with the industry to provide a set of guidelines to assist both security companies as well as security service buyers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can start by identifying key areas where technological solutions are clearly superior and seek to provide a set of common standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through specific funding support by the Government, we can bring down the cost of security technology solutions, improve productivity and enhance security outcomes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we need to consider mandating security assessments to optimise the use of technology and manpower.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is a Chinese saying: to get the task done, you first need the right tools.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us not wait until it is too late.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We have done so in the past through the Public Order Act and other legislation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We must remain vigilant and can look at these particular amendments.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Shangri-La shooting incident that Members had spoken about in the past is one such incident that we must have a clear response to.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We should never underestimate the importance of appropriate and even additional security measures, where necessary.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: However, Madam, I have certain concerns and, at the outset, I must say that my concerns are not with respect to anything that we would do which are anti-terrorist initiatives but are specifically about anything, including within these amendments, that may have an unwitting or an overt limitation on free speech or through censorship of the media.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we are seeking to stifle creativity, innovation or healthy intellectual debate as the Minister earlier alluded to, others may worry and I worry as well, Madam, that certain aspects and powers or even discretion that have now been put in the hands of the Police Commissioner and others may cause concern.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would ask the Minister, perhaps, how this categorisation would be delineated.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will the different classes of events be specifically clear and distinguished so that organisers will know and be certain as to what the classifications are and what may be their incumbent obligations?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this as well, Madam, because not every organiser may quite know what may be lying in store for them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This idea of not allowing any right to be heard, Madam, while there is no expressed duty to give reasons under Singapore's administrative law and I would not take issue with this, it does cause some concern.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister rightly mentioned earlier, even his declarations must be gazetted and it must show to members of the public what is being involved.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If the opportunity to be heard is being dispensed in some way, would there be a possibility for judicial review?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Would there be appeals to the Ministry itself if there is a legitimate reason as to why an event may go forward?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Could there be an appeal, perhaps, to the Police Commissioner to consider or reconsider this?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The next clause, Madam, that causes some concern is clause 9(g).

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It relates to the costs that will be involved regarding these events.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, will there be internal control mechanisms, Madam, to ascertain whether the expenses incurred by the Commissioner will be given effect to if the direction is reasonably incurred?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But the larger point would be, if we are seeking to impose obligations on event organisers with events that touch on political matters or political ends, we must have very clear directions at this stage so that we know what we are getting into.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Since coming into force in 2009, and subsequently with amendments made as recently as 2015, the Public Order Act (POA) has achieved its objectives to ensure order and safety in public spaces well.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As such, any proposed amendment should address specific gaps in public safety which have arisen.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It should also offer clear terms for the execution of the Act.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in my opinion, there are various aspects of the proposed amendments which require further clarification in terms of their intent.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the amendments will have an adverse impact on our efforts to encourage active citizenry.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our Government has made positive steps, particularly in recent years, to encourage citizens in policymaking.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Citizens should be politically aware and not politically naive.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Political discussion is important to let us understand why decisions are being made, how it affects others and, importantly, allow us to articulate the kind of governance we want.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When our citizens' trust and confidence in the political system grow, they will feel invested in the country's development and strategic direction.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, while we encourage political discourse and active citizenry, we would also agree that there must be terms of engagement that ensure civility, non-violence and public order.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I see the POA as an Act that assures meaningful engagement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, any policy change that deters citizens from becoming actively engaged will be counter-productive to our vision.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We know that there has been more and more active engagement through social media, but meaningful engagement done face to face is equally important.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: True active citizenry must also include Singaporeans initiating self-directed efforts in response to problems in our immediate surroundings.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Also, political discourse should not be seen as something scary and dangerous, or something that only articulates itself as complaining.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If people are afraid to participate openly in political discussions, they will not evolve into discerning citizens.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To date, I still have audience coming to me about my production and say: "Don't talk about such things.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hey, why are you making these criticisms, will you get questioned?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Don't do drama about politics, if not, you will get into trouble." How can all of us assure the public that there is nothing to fear?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Ironically, the amended POA might even further deter Singaporeans from good, solid political engagement and discussion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is in this light that I would like to examine and discuss this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: After all, the recommendations of such a panel may well include proposals for legislative changes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or how about a public lecture, organised by a local NGO, with a foreign expert speaking on healthy policy, proposing recommendations for Singapore to boost Singapore's birth rate?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That would also be covered under this very broad definition.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think the House can agree with me when I say these examples should certainly not fall afoul of POA.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: After all, they are beneficial for our nation, never mind that they deal with policy matters.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, they should not cause any public disorder or safety issues.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But the issue at hand is this: we cannot categorically claim such events have "a political end", nor can we say otherwise.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The amendment should then be clarified, to ensure such events are free from unnecessary scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If the proposed amendment is to deter foreigners from leading or participating in political events that threaten public order or safety, then is it repetitious?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because we have already dealt with such things adequately through clause 7(2) of POA.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What if there are contestations on the Commissioner's decision?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If the answer is that it can be challenged in Court, then it would definitely be a big deterrent for NGOs because of the cost involved.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: During the Budget Debate, I have spoken at length about how a strong civil society and an active citizenry build our national resilience.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are facing difficult and uncertain times ahead and, clearly, we do not have all the answers to the problems we face.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In such times, it benefits us to collaborate with and learn from international experts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our universities and Government agencies have always tapped on foreign resources.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our burgeoning civil society has much to learn as well from foreign experience and wisdom, so that it can grow more robust and address societal problems more effectively.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our nation as a whole has benefited greatly from an exchange of views with people from outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would such engagements now be in danger of ceasing, should the Commissioner, on his or her own discretion, deem them to be infringing the POA?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not believe I am alone in saying that the new amendments have the potential to incite more fear and create more barriers for civil society to engage with foreign experts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging that the Government wants to cultivate active citizenry.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But we should also not inhibit concerned individuals or civil society from initiating engagement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Bottom up is not always a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Top down also sometimes need to take a break.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is time for the Government to trust its people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let Singaporeans strive to find solutions for important issues without Government interference.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we feel more involved and invested in the future of our nation, then we can truly say Singapore has a genuine active citizenry.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Another clarification I would like to seek pertains to the Commissioner's decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is a very different power from that of deciding whether an event will potentially create public unrest.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, is the Commissioner the best judge of what is political and what is not?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, there is no dispute on the Commissioner's institutional expertise on what constitutes public disorder.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In giving the Commissioner this new responsibility, are we giving our Police Force the right to make political decisions?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would this not lead to questions about its impartiality?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I, for one, would not want public confidence in our Police Force to be eroded or its integrity questioned.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Even if the Commissioner is, indeed, impartial, with this new responsibility, he or she may have to make seemingly subjective decisions that favour certain groups and displease others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It would be hard to avoid accusations of political non-partisanship once the Commissioner has to make such difficult decisions outside of his or her institutional competence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This means that the Commissioner's decision would effectively be free from public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, without transparency in the decision-making process, the public has little option but to resort to speculation and conjecture.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of building our citizens' trust in the Police Force, the Bill could potentially cause an erosion of public confidence, which is something we do not want to see happen.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has been relatively safe so far, thanks to the vigilance of our security personnel as well as cooperation from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our years of effort at promoting mutual understanding and building tolerance and harmony amongst different racial, religious and community groups also play an important role.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, the threat of a terrorist attack is high and we must take pre-emptive measures to ensure the safety of Singapore and all our residents and visitors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also seek clarifications about whether this limit also applies to the Speakers' Corner, election rallies and events organised by grassroots organisations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on the minimum necessary security measures that an organiser must implement and how would the Government assist with the sharing of costs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or split events into two successive sessions, one immediately after the other with less than 5,000 within the venue while having less than 5,000 or just fall short of 5,000 waiting outside the venue, making a total of 5,000 at any point of time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also curious about whether the use of electronic and personal communication devices will be restricted at these events since they can be used by terrorists, as reported recently in the US and the European Union (EU).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The support of volunteer staff will help to reduce the cost of organising such events.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, will the Ministry consider constantly updating and equipping all NS personnel and reservists with skills and knowledge to combat terrorism?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarifications that will hopefully address the concerns of civil society groups, in particular, their concern that this Bill might have the unintended consequence of making it more difficult for civil society groups to responsibly and legitimately exercise their freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister had covered this earlier, but how will organisers determine that it is for free and non-ticketed events?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is very possible for an event to attract a greater turnout than expected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I personally experienced this when the Animal Concerns Research and Education Society (ACRES) held events at the Speakers' Corner when, at times, the turnout was twice of what we expected and catered for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Commissioner respond and how will security measures be implemented to ensure security in such a case?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, and more importantly, is there a possible loophole that organisers might simply report a lower number of the expected turnout?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With society evolving, topics that were once deemed contentious or taboo have, with time, become necessary conversations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Who decides when a matter becomes a matter of public controversy?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will it be an independent panel set up to make these decisions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Efforts to promote such conversations should not be penalised, and peaceful and constructive public gatherings are necessary ingredients for critical thinking, for active citizenry and for active participation in the Singapore story.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may not be a matter of public order or security, and it is not clear whether the Commissioner or the Singapore Police Force will have the institutional competence to make such a decision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In order to enforce the law properly, there must be public confidence in the Police Force which can only come if the Police are recognised to be politically neutral.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, there is potential for the Police's political neutrality to be compromised when they are required to make political decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Without detailed reasons, decisions by the Commissioner may lead to speculation which does not build public confidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Commissioner be required to provide organisers with reasons if their applications are rejected?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many civil society groups are also concerned about the financial costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I note that the Commissioner may direct organisers to implement security measures and traffic control under section 30(2)(f).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will affect events held at the Speakers' Corner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is important to consider if the affected group has the ability to pay for such security and traffic control measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NGOs and individuals acting on their own initiative may not be able to pay for enhanced security and traffic control measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I am fully supportive of the need for additional security measures, I am concerned about the ability of Singaporeans to hold events if they are going to be charged for being too popular.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like grants available for many programmes, is it possible to set up a grant to assist civil society groups with these costs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, Madam, can the Minister clarify if public consultations have been done with all relevant stakeholders, including civil society groups, with regard to this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, we must involve all stakeholders in this fight.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our unity as a nation is our greatest weapon against security threats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how organisers would predict the crowd turnout at free, non-ticketed events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had recognised that this will be a subjective exercise because they will have to plan for the venue, they will have to plan for logistics and, therefore, they will have an idea of what the crowd size will be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But a deliberate under-assessment, if that can be shown − of course, it has got to be shown by the prosecution − that is a different matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the example where you expect 4,999, I think all of us have some experience in organising events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would be surprised if the Police are not surprised that someone comes up and says "I expect 4,999".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that person can expect a more detailed assessment from the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked if the different classes of events we prescribe will be sufficiently clear and distinguished.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may refer to the specific clause, I think the Member was concerned about clause 3 in the new section 6A, "for the purposes of subsection 1, the Minister may prescribe the number of individuals for different classes of events".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the concern is, would there be good faith exercised?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, I would like to say to Members, we are trying to prescribe security for different types of events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Standing here today, you and I know different events will have different types of security signature.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An event relating to a concert will be very different from a public event that, say, intends to deal with issues of race or religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are matters that can only be decided based on the nature of the event, based also on international and regional events and surroundings, and then make an assessment, which is why it is difficult to prescribe upfront in the legislation, and which is why discretion has to be given to the Commissioner and the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the underlying rationale and principle of that particular clause is for the Commissioner to direct taking of specific security steps.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not to say: do not hold the event.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is to say, "Well, I think this event is going to require barricades, this event is going to require this kind of security, I think you better check the bags".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think it can be suggested that that exercise is going to be handled in bad faith.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Police will give the guidelines to the event organisers on what measures to be implemented, how the framework is to be implemented, and they will give examples, too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the "reasonable" expectation of the size of the crowd?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at past events, similar events, you look at what is the logistical planning for the event, and you look at the venue, as I have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, predicting the turnout accurately may be difficult and no one is saying that you have to be accurate, but you are required to make the best efforts to estimate the crowd size.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are all in this situation because of international events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not want what happened in Berlin, Nice or Istanbul to happen here, and so, everyone has got to play a part.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The vast majority of events at the Speakers' Corner will not attract this kind of threshold crowds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked about the costs involved where the organisers do not implement security and the Police step in to put in those measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the end, the Government is incurring the cost on behalf of the taxpayers of Singapore or, in fact, all citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Separately, non-compliance with the Commissioner's directions would be a criminal offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But really, we do not want to get there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want events to succeed, we want event organisers to work with the Police and to make sure that it is secure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everyone will have a great event, with as reasonable a framework as possible, and at as reasonable a cost as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if grants can be provided for civil society groups to pay for security measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have made the point that taxpayers are bearing a huge part of this cost already, in terms of what the Police have to do, in terms of providing for security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is now time for everyone in society to step up and bear different parts of the cost.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the question is how much should the taxpayer pay and how much should the event organiser pay?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is unfair to expect the general average citizen of Singapore to pay for every event 100% of the cost.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The citizens of Singapore are paying a very substantial part of the cost anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the need to ensure that security officers are well-trained to carry out their duties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is something that needs to be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My Ministry is working closely with the security industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we need to achieve is for the industry to offer high-quality services which offer the right quality and are sustainable from a manpower perspective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will consider Mr Melvyn Yong's suggestions on PWM and promoting greater use of technology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Greater use of technology is a no-brainer and we will obviously have to work on these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a second part which I said on the amendments which relates to foreigners using Singapore to promote political causes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, we have to bear in mind that the Act was first put in place several years ago in 2009.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we sought to do was to strike a balance between adequate space for political expression and society's need for order and stability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And by and large, that has been achieved and we have worked the Act quite successfully all these years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I sat listening to the very passionate speech by Nominated Member of Parliament Mr Kok Heng Leun but I wonder if we are moving like ships in the dark in the sea.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill says one thing and Mr Kok's speech pretty much has nothing to do with the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok said, "we have made positive steps to engage citizens in policymaking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Actively engaged citizenry is possible only with political discourse, involvement of the people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this, in turn, allows us to develop deeper understanding and our citizens' trust and confidence in the political system grow, they will feel invested in the country's development in strategic direction." Mr Kok also said it should not always be top-down and bottom-up; we have to trust our citizenry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of that, I do not think I disagree with and it would make a very good political speech at some point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what does that have to do with the amendments?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the amendments, in particular clause 4, and I do not know whether the Member has actually gone through clause 4.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 7(1) deals with the Commissioner receiving notice of the application and deciding whether to grant the permit or refuse to grant the permit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 2, which shows that the Commissioner has the discretion to refuse to grant a permit, may refuse to grant a permit, if the assembly or procession may occasion public disorder or damage to public property and so on − (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g) − all of that is not being amended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Kok has had no problems with any of those up to now; at least that has been the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The key condition is that this event is not being organised by a Singapore entity or individuals who are not citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, what has that got to do with bottom-up, top-down trust in citizenry, empowered citizenship?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, I would say, have more faith in our citizens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do not just hope for foreign involvement in organising events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why do we not have confidence that our people can organise and take part in civic activities?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, my Ministry made it clear that we will not agree to foreign participation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a Government, we do not take a position for or against Pink Dot.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we do take a position against foreign involvement in events like Pink Dot.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not new; that has always been the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We made that clear last year that, this year, we do not want to see foreign participation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the media, newspaper reports, Singapore companies have stepped up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I take no position, but the point is, this is a matter for Singaporeans, Singapore companies, Singapore entities to discuss without the involvement of foreign culture wars.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is the purpose of the amendment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The purpose of the amendment, therefore, actually fits in with what the Member said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is why I listened with some degree of perplexity as to what the thrust of the speech was.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, all these other points, the Member's question then is, for the ordinary Singaporean, is the amended POA going to deter him or her from good solid political engagement?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As you can see from the amendments, none of that is really germane.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Kok, if you do not mind, I would not deal with all other points that you have made along the same lines about local citizenry and active participation because that is not what this Bill deals with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You might say some of those points may potentially be relevant for the first part where there might be some increased costs, but that, I have explained, is necessary from a hard security perspective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But from the perspective of foreign involvement, I think I stand on very good grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said it is something that we need to bear in mind that foreign involvement may not just be the relatively innocent types where foreigners come in and take part or organise, but also directed by foreign state agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not think you will support that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think any Singaporean will support that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you distinguish between the one and the other?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is a cleaner rule to say foreigners, "Do not engage".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to whether that makes the Commissioner political, I will come back to it in a minute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The kind of events, even with a political dimension, if it does not involve foreigners, then it is not affected by these particular amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The balance between public space for political expression and social order and stability is really different when it comes to foreigners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member mentioned the context of, say, animal welfare.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Malaysians finance an event in Singapore and take part in an event in Singapore and encourage Singaporeans to come and take part in an event in Singapore which says that Syariah law should be imposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you think we should agree to Malaysians taking part and financing the event?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say foreign Christian groups, say, financed from America, come here, want to organise an event combined with locals, and they want to call it an anti-lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) rally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you think we should agree to that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They want to organise an event in Singapore and combine with our Buddhists, and they want to protest against the Rohingyas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been successful by being very firm about that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In India, there are states which now ban the slaughter of cows.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hindus, particularly, targeted at Muslim sellers of meat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing under the rubric of animal welfare, Hindus from India want to finance an animal welfare event in Singapore protesting against the selling of beef in Singapore and they want to involve Singapore Hindus, and it is targeted at groups along the lines of people who sell or eat such meat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they say that this whole thing is animal welfare.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you see, this has shades of complexity and any attempt to define upfront political event and a non-political event will run into these shades of complexity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All you will end up doing is creating many alley ways and bye ways in which your definition would be made useless and you would be made a laughing stock.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in this field, to define this with absolute clarity in the way that you want, first, the reasons for wanting them, I assure you, is not quite what the Bill seeks to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not seek to cut back on Singaporean rights in the context of these amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the absolute clarity that you seek, if we try to define it, it is not going to achieve what we want to achieve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, really, then it becomes a question of philosophy which then touches on a little bit on what Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan talked about as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you have to trust the Commissioner of Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ninety percent of Singaporeans trust the Police, as I read from another survey to this House a few weeks ago.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The alternative is then to run to Court each time somebody is not happy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not the way you can run a proper Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way we have run the Government, successfully and cleanly with the right outcomes, has been to vest the discretion in many areas in the Executive, with the knowledge that a highly-educated population will hold the Executive to account if there is abuse of that power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the context here, we are specifically dealing with a Commissioner looking at an event and saying that it is political, political ends, involving foreigners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think Singaporeans will argue with this, of giving the Commissioner the discretion to make that assessment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One that deals with the welfare of dogs and kittens may pass muster.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One that deals with the welfare of cows, specifically in terms of slaughter or eating its meat, may not pass muster.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends, may or may not pass muster.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Depends on who is involved, depends on what is the purpose and depends on who is financing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the basic question: in the absence of the possibility of being able to define it without becoming ridiculous, then you have to vest that discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You vest that discretion, you give that framework, and it works.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the rest for that section, that is the way that section is now re-worked in respect of foreign participation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Commissioner declares an event to be a political event, that does not make him political.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is not deciding in favour of one conclusion or another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has to make an assessment based on the provisions as to whether it is directed towards political ends, regardless of how that question is to be answered, as in it may go in favour of this political end or that political end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His is a threshold question: does it involve politics or political ends?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also, Mr Kok Heng Leun was concerned that the amendments somehow restrict civil society's access to foreign expertise and knowledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most of the avenues for civil society to tap on the foreign expertise and knowledge are untouched.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are now only dealing with public assemblies and processions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there continues to be plenty of avenues for civil society to learn from others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those are assessments that he has got to make.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were also questions on what might be a matter of public controversy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is contained and also considered in the Films Act as to what is a political matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan made the specific point as to whether this will stifle free speech by reference to clause 3, which gives the discretion for different numbers and different events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the Commissioner's discretion under clause 4 and his powers to modify, I have explained how it works.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People have to make an assessment as to what numbers they expect and they come to the Commissioner within the prescribed period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then the Commissioner makes an assessment that tells them that these are the measures I want you to put in place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to whether there is a recourse from the Commissioner's decision to not grant a permit for an assembly or procession, the existing section 11 allows a person who is aggrieved by a Commissioner's decision to appeal to the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is that appeal process and the Minister can allow the appeal either in whole or in part.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, if I have not, I am sure Members will let me know.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: First, I want to make a clarification that in my speech, my concern was about what if local NGOs would sometimes, because of capacity-building purpose, need foreign participation, in terms of foreign speakers in their public assembly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I share the Minister's position that we should not have foreign entities organising such events here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: On that point, I will agree with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, I think my question here is that, as long as there is enough clarification so that civil society can feel that they can still continue with what they are doing, I think that would be really very good.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I just want to check with the Minister, in a particular case whereby, for example, an NGO, which already has a staff member who is a foreigner and he is working full-time with the NGO and they happen to be organising a particular event, would that actually be a problem under this new amendment?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, Mr Kok, it is a bit difficult to answer that question in a vacuum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on what role that foreigner plays.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of foreign agencies − when I say agencies, you know what type of agencies I am referring to − if they are going to put up their hand and have a signature, it will be through NGOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you will see I have taken some trouble to take you through the amendments that, and as I have said, I think the Bill that is presented and your speech pass each other by, like ships in the night, because they are not engaging with each other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because your speech was about Singaporeans, Singaporean civil society, we should not have top-down; we should have bottom-up; we should encourage Singaporeans; we should make sure that our people participate and I said that I agree entirely with you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that has nothing to do with clause 4.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the best example I can give you, as I gave in my wrap-up speech, is again Pink Dot.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, when my Ministry said no foreign participation, there was considerable concern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were these arguments about what amounts to politics because my Ministry issued a statement saying that we have always taken the position that foreigners cannot engage in political activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In our view, LGBT issues are for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were these, what I would call, issues around the definition of politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, there was concern that when we say no to foreign sponsorship, for example, for Pink Dot, it will impact on the event.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But actually, as you see, based on media reports, Singaporeans are stepping up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, the Government is neutral on this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But whether it is pro-LGBT or opposing LGBT, it is a matter for Singaporeans to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Singapore companies, Singaporean sponsors are stepping up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I would say, tell your friends, the civic society, have some confidence in themselves and have confidence in Singaporeans to step up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be difficult to stand here and give you a clear black line that it applies to this and it does not apply to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Apart from anything else, a particular event held in one set of circumstances, domestic and regional and international, may take a completely different complexion when the regional and international circumstances change and domestic situations change, which is why these are matters where you will have to give the power to the Executive and let the Executive decide.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Yes, I am actually very happy that the Pink Dot has been able to get all the support locally.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And I also want to reiterate, which is one of our fellow Members' points, that it is important that Singaporeans organise it and we have our say.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: But I think here the concern is with regard to how the Commissioner is going to make the decision.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Members have actually suggested would they have an independent committee to help them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A weak government without the desire to decide these things will pass it on to a judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it will result in the matters constantly being mitigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our people will know whether the decision is being exercised properly or improperly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if we keep making decisions improperly, any government will face the consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I say is subject to some applicable principles on judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You say why should it be the Commissioner of Police?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another panel, an independent panel, something that is independent of the Police, I presume, advising the Commissioner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is that panel going to do that you think the Commissioner is not able to do himself?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And really, all of these are suggestions to dilute the exercise of power or the authority of the Commissioner of Police which the Bill seeks to vest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said our approach to governance has been to vest to that authority and say that person will be responsible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, and there plenty of examples, where you have panels which either outside of the Statutory Board or Executive, which either advise or sometimes, actually make a decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that relate usually to matters of morality, taste, what the public might find acceptable or not acceptable in terms of social mores.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is this an event that may have security implications?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is this an event where I should allow foreigners to take part?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why the people elect us − to make those decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we get it wrong, the people will tell us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am not saying no to public advising the Executive, but I think there is a range of areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some where clearly the public panel should advise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think this is one of those.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I am sorry but just one last point to reiterate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Minister, I think a lot of civil societies also want to build their trust with the Government.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I think it goes a long way for both sides to work together.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And with regard to this Bill, I hope that, if there were actually more consultations in the process, that would actually clarify a lot of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, what I can hope is that you, with your contacts with the civil society, will explain to them what I have explained to you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is absolutely important to have that trust between citizens and the Government, and also civil society and the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thankfully, Singapore, in the context of the overall plunge in trust in government in the rest of the world, we are in a fairly, in fact, quite healthy position in terms of how much the people trust the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to make sure that we work very hard to maintain that trust, because trust cannot be demanded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you have got to continue to prove that you are worthy of the trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill, our own view, looking at it is that when people see clause 4, first of all we did not think there was any issue of trust when it came to the Commissioner of Police directing that an event shall include extra security measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It did not strike me at all that this would raise any questions of trust with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may affect − now that I have listened to you − the people who misunderstand the scope of the Bill and so I think it is the Government's duty to go out and explain what this Bill covers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To that extent, thank you for helping us.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.51 pm until 5.10 pm.
